newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss stocks seen supported despite early losses.
newsitem.headline: Swiss stocks seen supported despite early losses.

text.p: Swiss stocks began under pressure following sharp losses in U.S. stocks on Friday, but analysts did not expect landslide losses on Monday.
The blue-chip Swiss Market Index (SMI) SMI dropped sharply at Monday's open at 0800 GMT, dipping by over 3.5 percent in the first few minutes of trade.
But it edged up from initial lows to trade down about 137 points at 5,361, off 2.5 percent, at 0920 GMT.

Reinhard Stutz, technical research analyst and vice president at Bank Julius Baer, said that next support for the SMI was likely to be 5,250. That level was near Monday's early low of 5,278.3, down 220.2 points from Friday's close.
"At the moment, we are certainly in a correction, and at the same time near the 50 percent retracement from the last upmove -- that is, the start of the uptrend in April to early July," Stutz said.
He saw the next key level further down was 5,020, which represented a 62 percent retracement. The Swiss market's all-time high was set July 9, at 6,101.2.

"There is no reason to panic. The decline at the opening was quite strong. But the move was mainly in cash, while the futures contract (SMI futures SMIU7 ) held up relatively well," said Gerd Ramsperger, analyst at Zuercher Kantonalbank.
Ramsperger also saw support for the SMI at 5,250.
At the same time, he did not rule out some shifting into bonds, as institutional investors moved assets out of stocks.
The SMI dropped about six percent last week.
This compared with the Dow Jones industrial average's drop of 6.8 percent by Friday, from an all-time closing high of 8,259.31 on August 6.
Some Swiss analysts blamed latest declines on nervousness about U.S. and German interest rates.
Activity is likely to remain nervous in Europe, due to uncertainty about the long-term outlook for interest rates.
But analysts noted that at the same time stocks sold off on Monday morning, debt prices were actually firmer, following a late recovery in U.S. Treasury bonds on Friday.
In the U.S. and Germany, most analysts do not seem to expect any imminent rate rises.
The Federal Reserve holds its regular Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday.

The Bundesbank also meets on Thursday for the first time since its summer break, and German economists say the Bundesbank has prepared markets for an eventual rate increase, although most do not expect this step as soon as Thursday.

Swiss interest rates are also seen holding steady near-term, with any tightening at the moment appearing unlikely. The Swiss National Bank has said it will keep the domestic money market liquid to prevent the Swiss franc from appreciating to a point where it could harm exports.
